title: Methohexital -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Methohexital is a short-acting barbiturate anesthetic agent used in anesthesia and procedural sedation, valued for its rapid onset and brief duration of action. This activity focuses on the indications, pharmacologic actions, and contraindications of methohexital, with a detailed review of its mechanism of action, pharmacokinetics, dosing principles, adverse effect profile, and clinically relevant drug interactions. A comprehensive understanding of methohexital provides healthcare professionals with a strong scientific foundation for its practical use, supporting appropriate patient selection, careful dosing, vigilant monitoring, and effective risk mitigation while minimizing adverse effects during anesthetic care.

title: Methohexital -- Continuing Education Activity
content: The participant gains evidence-based knowledge necessary for the safe and effective administration of methohexital in clinical practice. This continuing education activity emphasizes informed decision-making regarding dosing, monitoring, and recognizing potential complications. Notably, the emphasis lies on empowering healthcare professionals by highlighting the essential role of the interprofessional healthcare team in methohexital management. Collaboration among anesthesiologists, nurses, pharmacists, and procedural staff enhances patient outcomes by improving communication, coordinating medication preparation and administration, monitoring physiologic responses, and responding promptly to adverse events. By clarifying professional roles and fostering coordinated collaboration, this activity equips healthcare professionals with practical tools that support procedural safety, individualized care, and improved clinical outcomes associated with methohexital use.

title: Methohexital -- Indications
content: Methohexital belongs to a family of drugs known as barbiturates. [1] Methohexital sodium is a highly potent, ultra–short-acting methylated barbiturate with approximately 2.5 times the hypnotic effect of thiopental. [2]

title: Methohexital -- Indications -- Food and Drug Administration–Approved Indications
content: Methohexital is approved for intravenous induction of anesthesia before the administration of other general anesthetic agents. Methohexital is also indicated as an intravenous anesthetic agent for short diagnostic, surgical, or therapeutic procedures associated with minimal painful stimulation and for the induction of a hypnotic state. Methohexital may be used for intravenous induction and as an adjunct to subpotent inhalational anesthetic agents, such as nitrous oxide in oxygen, for short surgical procedures. In combination with other parenteral agents, typically narcotic analgesics, methohexital may be used to supplement subpotent inhalational anesthetic agents during longer surgical procedures. Methohexital is also approved by the Food and Drug Administration for pediatric patients older than 1 month for rectal/intramuscular induction of anesthesia. In pediatric patients, it is also approved for short therapeutic, surgical, and diagnostic procedures associated with minimal painful stimuli. [3] [4]

title: Methohexital -- Indications -- Off-Label Uses
content: Methohexital is a preferred agent for use in electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). [5] [6] [7] [8] Methohexital is the choice of sedative in ECT as it both reduces the seizure threshold and prolongs seizure duration. The latter is an important quality during ECT, as seizure duration is linked to improved ECT efficacy. [9] [10] [11] However, its use has also been shown to be useful in procedural sedation for cardioversion, as an induction agent for intubation in neonates, and as a sedative during imaging procedures. [12] [13] [14]

title: Methohexital -- Mechanism of Action
content: Methohexital produces its effect by enhancing the inhibitory actions of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) at the GABA-A receptor. [15] At higher concentrations, it can directly stimulate and activate the receptor. Barbiturates bind to the GABA-A receptor and increase the open duration of the GABA-A receptor without having any effect on channel opening frequency or conductance. Specifically, the downstream effect is on the chloride channel, keeping it open longer and leading to an influx of chloride. This action activates inhibitory pathways in the brain, reducing neuronal excitability and inducing anesthesia or sedation. [16] [15]  Research has shown the highest concentration of methohexital in the hypothalamus, globus pallidus, and the substantia nigra. Once the GABA-A receptor is activated, increased chloride influx increases the negative charge inside the membrane, resulting in hyperpolarization and thus post-synaptic neuron inhibition. [17]

title: Methohexital -- Mechanism of Action
content: Methohexital is derived from barbituric acid, which is a compound made of malonic acid and urea. The chemical formula for methohexital is 1-methyl-2-pentynyl barbituric acid. The acyclic side chain at the fifth carbon of the benzene ring is responsible for the hypnotic activity of this compound. Additionally, compared to barbituric acid, methohexital has a methylated nitrogen, which produces excitatory effects but also causes a rapid onset and short duration of action, making this drug clinically useful. [17]

title: Methohexital -- Mechanism of Action -- Pharmacokinetics
content: Absorption: After intravenous administration of methohexital, peak brain concentrations occur at 30 seconds and then steadily decline as the drug redistributes to other tissues. Approximately 5 minutes after administration, about half of the initial concentration is in the central nervous system. The duration of action for methohexital is 4 to 7 minutes. The bioavailability of methohexital following rectal administration is 17%. Intravenous administration of methohexital results in rapid uptake by the brain (within 30 seconds) and rapid induction of sleep. Following intramuscular administration to pediatric patients, the onset occurs within 2 to 10 minutes. Following rectal administration to pediatric patients, sleep onset occurs within 5 to 15 minutes.

title: Methohexital -- Mechanism of Action -- Pharmacokinetics
content: Distribution: Methohexital does not appear to concentrate in fat depots to the extent of other barbiturate anesthetic agents. Thus, cumulative effects are fewer and recovery is more rapid with methohexital than with thiobarbiturates such as thiopental (thiopentone). The plasma protein binding is approximately 79%.

title: Methohexital -- Mechanism of Action -- Pharmacokinetics
content: Metabolism: Methohexital is metabolized in the liver through oxidation and demethylation. [2] Side-chain oxidation of methohexital is the most important biotransformation step, in which the molecule undergoes oxidation at carbon 5 of the benzene ring, resulting in the inactive metabolite hydroxymethohexital. In summary, the disappearance of methohexital from the bloodstream is attributable to both hepatic inactivation and redistribution, with redistribution playing a greater role. [17] Excretion: Methohexital is excreted by glomerular filtration. [18]

title: Methohexital -- Administration -- Available Dosage Forms and Strengths
content: Methohexital is available for rectal, intravenous, and intramuscular administration. Intravenous and rectal intermittent administration: Methohexital 1% solution (10 mg/mL) Continuous intravenous administration: Methohexital 0.2% solution (2 mg/mL) Intramuscular administration: Methohexital 5% solution (50 mg/mL)

title: Methohexital -- Administration -- Dosing
content: Standard adult dosing for anesthesia induction is 50 to 120 mg intravenously as a bolus. General anesthesia maintenance calls for 20 to 40 mg intravenous every 4 to 7 minutes as needed. In pediatrics, the induction dose of general anesthesia is 6.6 to 10 mg/kg intramuscularly, given as a single dose. Alternatively, 25 mg/kg as a single dose rectally is an option.

title: Methohexital -- Administration -- Dosing
content: In pediatric patients, methohexital has been used for procedural sedation to obtain imaging at doses ranging from 0.5 to 2.0 mg/kg. [19] Rectal methohexital is predominantly used in the pediatric population; one study reported that a dose of 30 mg/kg of 10% methohexital induced sleep in 85% of children. [20] The induction dose of methohexital for ECT is 1.5 mg/kg. [21]

title: Methohexital -- Administration -- Specific Patient Populations
content: Hepatic impairment: No dosage adjustments are provided in the product labeling. However, because methohexital undergoes hepatic metabolism, dose modification may be necessary. Methohexital should be used with caution in patients with hepatic impairment. Renal impairment: No dose adjustment is provided in the product labeling.

title: Methohexital -- Administration -- Specific Patient Populations
content: Pregnancy considerations: There are no adequate and well-controlled studies of methohexital use in pregnant patients. Data from pregnant nonhuman primates suggest that exposure to anesthetic and sedative agents that block N -methyl-D-aspartate receptors and potentiate GABA activity during periods of peak brain development, particularly when administered for longer than 3 hours, can induce neuronal apoptosis in the offspring's brain. In animal reproduction studies, methohexital administered at doses up to approximately 4 to 7 times the recommended human dose did not demonstrate evidence of direct fetal harm. Methohexital has been used for cesarean delivery; however, due to its aqueous solubility and low protein binding, it readily and rapidly crosses the placenta, leading to fetal and neonatal exposure. Methohexital should be used during pregnancy only when the expected clinical benefit outweighs the potential risk. Prolonged or repeated anesthetic exposures should be avoided when feasible. In ECT, the standard induction drugs in pregnancy are methohexital or propofol due to their rapid onset of action and quick clearance from the fetal circulation. [22] Careful maternal-fetal risk-benefit assessment and multidisciplinary perinatal planning are advised.

title: Methohexital -- Administration -- Specific Patient Populations
content: Breastfeeding considerations: Methohexital concentrations in breast milk are minimal. Available data indicate that no waiting period is required before resuming breastfeeding following a single maternal dose. Breastfeeding may be resumed once the mother has recovered sufficiently from anesthesia. When methohexital is administered as part of a multimodal anesthetic regimen, breastfeeding recommendations should follow guidance for the anesthetic drug with the most significant potential risk. Based on available pharmacokinetic data, an infant receives a maximum single dose of approximately 0.04 mg of methohexital in a 100 mL feeding, administered 1 hour after maternal administration, corresponding to approximately 0.1% to 0.8% of the maternal weight-adjusted dose. [23] Caution should be exercised when considering methohexital administration in a breastfeeding mother.

title: Methohexital -- Administration -- Specific Patient Populations
content: Older patients: Older patients may generally have conditions in which methohexital should be used cautiously, such as hypertension or hypotension, preexisting circulatory compromise, myocardial ischemia, heart failure, and obstructive lung disease. Caution should be exerted in debilitated patients or in those with impaired renal, hepatic, or cardiovascular function. Barbiturates may affect the metabolism of other concomitantly used drugs commonly taken by senior adults, such as anticoagulants and steroids. Therapy should be initiated at a lower dosage, given the above-mentioned pathologies and polypharmacy.

title: Methohexital -- Adverse Effects
content: The adverse effects of methohexital include respiratory depression, apnea, hiccups, cardiovascular depression, and laryngospasm. [17] In critically ill preload-dependent patients, methohexital may reduce systemic vascular resistance and cardiac output; however, the incidence of these events is low. [24] The ventilatory and cardiovascular depressant effects of methohexital are dose-dependent; however, they vary with the patient's preexisting disease. The respiratory depressant effect may result from both central and peripheral mechanisms. Methohexital can alter upper airway tone, leading to obstruction, and affect the brainstem respiratory centers, resulting in apnea and hypoventilation. Hypotension has also been noted during methohexital administration and is mediated by peripheral vasodilation, resulting in decreased afterload and preload and a negative inotropic effect on the heart. Methohexital is commonly associated with pain when injected into smaller veins. A study demonstrated that dissolving the drug in a lipid emulsion before administration resulted in pain resolution with no change in potency. [25] Mean arterial pressure is not significantly affected after administration of methohexital and appears to be more hemodynamically stable when compared to other agents. [26] As methohexital is a commonly used agent during ECT, it is essential to note that it has dose-dependent anticonvulsant properties and may adversely affect seizure procurement in a subset of patients with high seizure thresholds. [27]

title: Methohexital -- Adverse Effects -- Drug-Drug Interactions
content: Solutions of methohexital intravenous injection should not be mixed in the same syringe or administered through the same needle with acid solutions such as atropine sulfate, succinylcholine chloride, or metocurine iodide. Changes in pH can cause free barbituric acid to precipitate. The solubility of sodium salts of barbiturates, including methohexital sodium, is maintained only in relatively high alkaline pH conditions. Prior chronic barbiturates or phenytoin administration may reduce the clinical effectiveness of methohexital. This reduced response is attributed to pharmacodynamic tolerance to barbiturate anesthetics and increased hepatic metabolic capacity, resulting in more rapid clearance and diminished hypnotic effect. Barbiturates may also alter the disposition of other concomitantly administered medications, including corticosteroids, ethyl alcohol, propylene glycol–containing solutions, and anticoagulants. Concomitant use requires caution and dose adjustment.

title: Methohexital -- Adverse Effects
content: Methohexital should not be mixed with Lactated Ringer's injection, as its pH and calcium content may cause precipitation or reduced stability. Methohexital should be reconstituted and administered only with compatible diluents as recommended in the product labeling. Importantly, when methohexital is administered in conjunction with other medications, such as opioids, the cardiorespiratory depressant effects may be synergistic. Adverse reactions, including restlessness, excitation, and delirium, have been reported. In some cases, these effects may respond to intravenous caffeine; however, such treatment should be used with caution. [28]

title: Methohexital -- Contraindications
content: Barbiturates, such as methohexital, are contraindicated in acute intermittent porphyria. [29] Acute intermittent porphyria is a deficiency of the enzyme hydroxymethylbilane synthase in the pathway for heme biosynthesis. Acute attacks are typically sporadic and manifest as severe abdominal pain, peripheral neuropathy, psychiatric symptoms, autonomic dysfunction, and hyponatremia. Methohexital is strictly contraindicated in patients with a history of acute intermittent porphyria. [30] Prior hypersensitivity to barbiturates is also a contraindication to methohexital. [31]

title: Methohexital -- Contraindications -- Box Warnings
content: Methohexital must be administered only in hospital or ambulatory care settings equipped for continuous respiratory monitoring, including pulse oximetry, and cardiac monitoring. Immediate availability of resuscitative drugs is essential. Appropriate airway equipment for bag-valve-mask ventilation and intubation, sized to the patient's age and body habitus, must be on hand. Personnel trained in airway management and resuscitation should be present throughout administration. For deep sedation, continuous monitoring by a designated individual other than the proceduralist is mandatory to ensure patient safety.

title: Methohexital -- Contraindications -- Precautions/Warnings
content: Pediatric neurotoxicity: Animal studies have shown that anesthetic and sedative agents that antagonize N -methyl-D-aspartate receptors or GABA activity can increase neuronal apoptosis in the developing central nervous system and can be associated with long-term cognitive deficits (when administered for durations exceeding 3 hours). The clinical importance of these findings in humans remains uncertain. The period of vulnerability appears to correspond to exposures from the third trimester of gestation through the first several months after birth. Pediatric neurotoxicity may persist for approximately 3 years in humans. However, sedative or anesthetic drugs are necessary for pediatric patients requiring surgery. Appropriate risk-benefit evaluation is needed. Further, well-controlled clinical investigations are warranted. [32]

title: Methohexital -- Contraindications
content: Intra-arterial injection: An intra-arterial methohexital administration can result in necrosis and gangrene, which may require amputation. If extravasation is reported during methohexital injection, the infusion should be discontinued. The early use of subcutaneous enoxaparin at standard prophylactic dosing, along with close neurovascular monitoring and warm compresses, is recommended to decrease thrombotic complications and progression of tissue damage. [33] Intra-arterial steroid injection at the site of injury, followed by systemic steroids, is also suggested.

title: Methohexital -- Monitoring
content: When administering methohexital, it is crucial to know that respiratory and hemodynamic effects may occur. Continuous monitoring throughout the procedure and recovery period is essential. Guidelines from various organizations emphasize that anesthesia monitoring standards must be upheld, with the most critical requirement being the presence of a dedicated individual whose sole responsibility is to monitor the patient and manage sedation. Monitors, including a hemodynamic (blood pressure cuff), O 2 saturation (continuous pulse oximetry), electrocardiogram, end-tidal CO 2 , and respiratory rate, should be in place.

title: Methohexital -- Toxicity -- Signs and Symptoms of Overdose
content: Toxicity following intravenous overdose of methohexital occurs within seconds of administration. When administered rectally or ingested, the onset of toxicity may be delayed. Clinical manifestations of ultrashort-acting barbiturates, such as methohexital overdose, include central nervous system depression, respiratory depression, hypotension with decreased peripheral vascular resistance, and neuromuscular excitability. Severe overdose may result in circulatory collapse, pulmonary edema, and cardiac arrest. High doses of methohexital are associated with seizures in the postoperative period, likely due to acute withdrawal, as it is highly potent. Other symptoms of toxicity include muscle twitching, apnea, and shivering. [34]

title: Methohexital -- Toxicity -- Management of Overdose
content: Management of methohexital overdose is primarily supportive. Immediate priorities include airway protection, adequate oxygenation, and ventilatory support. Continuous monitoring of vital signs, blood gases, and serum electrolytes is recommended. Hypotension should be treated with intravenous fluids and positional support, followed by vasopressors or inotropic agents as indicated. Seizures should be treated with intravenous benzodiazepines, with phenytoin as adjunctive therapy; refractory seizures may require general anesthesia and neuromuscular blockade. Consultation with a regional poison control center or medical toxicologist is recommended to guide management, particularly in cases of severe poisoning, suspected coingestants, or atypical clinical courses. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Barbiturate Toxicity ," for further information.

title: Methohexital -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Methohexital is a barbiturate, and while it is a beneficial agent in its applications, it is not without risks. Hence, the entire interprofessional health team has to coordinate its activities when using this drug. The ordering clinician decides whether to use the drug and its dose, whereas the pharmacist must verify the dose and check for potential drug interactions. Nursing monitors and administers the drug and reports any unusual circumstances to clinicians or pharmacists. With a collaborative approach, methohexital can be a safe anesthetic agent that helps the team achieve positive patient outcomes.
